title: The Shift from Chatbots to Long-Horizon Agents

questions.question: With a 14-hour baseline and a 7-month doubling time, what horizon does horizon_at report at month 14?
questions.explanation: Two doubling intervals have elapsed, so 14 * 2^(14/7) = 14 * 4 = 56 hours.

questions.question: What does end_to_end_reliability(0.99, 70) imply about a 70-step agent run?
options: About 70% reliability, so it is production-ready
About 49% reliability, which the demo labels coin-flip or worse
Exactly 99% reliability because each step is independent
A reliability above 99% because errors average out
questions.explanation: The function raises the per-step probability to the number of steps: 0.99^70 is about 0.495, so long chains compound small failures.

questions.question: What is the largest integer step count max_steps_for_target(0.99, 0.5) can return?
questions.explanation: It floors log(0.5) / log(0.99), which is about 68.97, yielding 68 steps.

questions.question: A 168-hour horizon has a 40% deployment gap. What effective horizon does the demo compute?
questions.explanation: The gap multiplier is 1 - 0.40, so 168 * 0.60 = 100.8 hours.

questions.question: Using the lesson's 14-hour baseline and 7-month doubling time, when does the horizon first reach 168 hours?
questions.explanation: The target is twelve times the baseline, so months_to_cross returns 7 * log2(12), about 25.1 months.

questions.question: How should the demo classify 0.995 per-step reliability over 200 steps?
options: Production-ready because the step rate exceeds 99%
About 37% end-to-end reliability, so coin flip or worse
About 37% end-to-end reliability, so not production
Exactly 0.5 because the target is 200 steps
questions.explanation: 0.995^200 is about 0.367, which is below 0.5, so the runtime label is coin flip or worse; it is also below the 0.80 production threshold.
